question: What goes wrong with Linux epoll edge-triggered mode (EPOLLET), and which common beliefs about it are false? Find: lost wakeups from partial reads; blocking descriptors under edge-triggered mode; starvation; thundering herd; events from a closed file descriptor whose open file description is still open; EPOLLONESHOT re-arm races; the belief that a "short read" always means the file is drained; the belief that edge-triggered mode fires only on an empty-to-non-empty transition; and any kernel change or regression that altered edge-triggered wake-up behaviour (with the kernel versions).

sources.rank_basis: tier B: class (LWN.net, an edited kernel-news publication; article by Jonathan Corbet, whom the LWN FAQ lists as 'Executive Editor, Kernel coverage', line 166 of the provenance page = vetted engineering literature). The reader comments under the article are unvetted; facts taken from them say so in their summary
tier B: class (personal blog of Marek Majkowski)
tier B: class (personal blog of Marek Majkowski)

tier B: class (linux-kernel mailing-list thread, 58 messages by many authors; community posts, so the higher number of the ranks that fit). Davide Libenzi's own messages in it are not rated separately

facts.summary: A 2019 pipe fix changed pipe writes from always waking waiting readers to waking them only when the pipe buffer was empty at the start of the write.
facts.quote: The 2019 fix changed the way that wakeup was performed. Before, a write to a pipe would unconditionally wake any waiting readers; indeed, it could wake them multiple times in a single system call. The fix changed this behavior to only perform the wakeup if the pipe buffer was empty at the start of the operation; a write to a pipe that already contained data waiting to be read would simply add the new data without causing the wakeup.

facts.summary: The fix to the 2019 pipe rework (Torvalds's fix for the GNU make slowdown) went in just before the 5.5 kernel was released.
facts.quote: a fix by Linus Torvalds was applied that made the problem go away. The 5.5 kernel was released shortly afterward,

facts.summary: After that change, a process starting an edge-triggered wait on a pipe that already held data would not see an edge and would not wake when more data arrived.
facts.quote: A process requesting an edge-triggered wait will not see an immediate return from epoll_wait() if there is available data; instead, it will wait until the situation changes. At least, that is how it worked before the 2019 patches. Once the pipe driver stopped performing wakeups any time that data arrived, processes initiating edge-triggered waits when there was already data available would not see the "edge" and would not wake.

facts.summary: Android libraries such as Realm relied on getting an edge-triggered wakeup for each write even when the pipe already held data; they broke when kernel 5.10 shipped in the Android 12 beta.
facts.quote: There are a number of Android libraries, such as Realm, that depend on getting edge-triggered wakeups even if there had been data waiting in the pipe before the epoll_wait() call was made. The purpose, evidently, is to wait until the pipe buffer is full, then read all of the data in a single operation. Those libraries broke when the 5.10 kernel went into the Android 12 beta, bringing down a set of apps with them.

facts.summary: Torvalds, quoted in the article, defines an edge as a change from no data to some data, not as a further write adding more data.
facts.quote: An edge is not "somebody wrote more data". An edge is "there was no data, now there is data". … A level-triggered signal is simply "there is data".

facts.summary: The regression was fixed anyway: merged for 5.14-rc4 and backported to 5.10.56 and 5.13.8; the fix does not fully restore the old behaviour, doing only one wakeup per write.
facts.quote: a new fix that was merged for 5.14-rc4 at the end of July and was included in the 5.10.56 and 5.13.8 stable updates. This patch does not quite restore the old behavior; specifically, it will only perform one wakeup per write operation.

facts.summary: The regression shipped with 5.5 (January 2020), lasted about a year and a half and reached the 5.10 long-term-stable release.
facts.quote: The 5.5 kernel was released in January 2020 … This regression thus endured for a year and a half, and found its way into the 5.10 long-term-stable release last December.

facts.summary: After the fix, Intel's test system reported hackbench nearly 13% slower; Torvalds posted another patch restoring closer-to-old wakeups only when the pipe is used with a polling call.
facts.quote: there is already a report (from Intel's automated test system) that the hackbench benchmark regressed by nearly 13% after the latest fix was applied. … he posted a new patch that provides something closer to the older behavior — but only if the pipe is being used with one of the polling functions.

facts.summary: Reader comment by mkerrisk (not the article): epoll(7) itself says edge-triggered epoll can generate multiple events for multiple chunks of data, which he takes as an argument against Torvalds's definition of an edge.
facts.quote: Since even with edge-triggered epoll, multiple events can be generated upon receipt of multiple chunks of data, the caller has the option to specify the EPOLLONESHOT flag … As I argued in Oct 2020, the existence of EPOLLONESHOT is, in my estimation, an argument against Linus's interpretation.

facts.summary: Reader comment by mkerrisk (not the article): every other mechanism he tested (Internet stream sockets, POSIX message queues, terminals, nested epoll) behaves the way pipes did under EPOLLET before the change.
facts.quote: In fact, every other mechanism that I tested (Internet domain stream sockets, POSIX message queues, terminals, hierarchical epoll) behaves the same as EPOLLET historically behaved for epoll.

facts.summary: Reader comment by NYKevin quoting epoll(7): an EPOLLET application should use non-blocking descriptors, since a blocking read or write can starve a task handling many descriptors, and should wait only after read or write returns EAGAIN.
facts.quote: An application that employs the EPOLLET flag should use … nonblocking file descriptors to avoid having a blocking read or … write starve a task that is handling multiple file descriptors. … by waiting for an event only after read(2) or write(2) return … EAGAIN.

facts.summary: Reader comment by NYKevin: waiting only after EAGAIN is safe without EPOLLONESHOT because an event is still queued; with EPOLLONESHOT he says you must re-arm before read/write, leaving a race in which duplicate notifications can still arrive.
facts.quote: there is a race between read(2)/write(2) returning EAGAIN and you calling epoll_wait(2), during which more data could become available. This is safe as long as you don't use EPOLLONESHOT, because an event will still be generated even if you are not waiting for it (and then epoll_wait will return immediately). But if you use EPOLLONESHOT, then you have to re-arm the epoll before calling read or write to avoid the race, which renders the whole thing rather pointless because now you have another race between epoll_ctl and read/write, where you can still receive duplicate notifications anyway.

facts.summary: Reader comment by comex: when a descriptor is added or re-enabled with epoll_ctl, the kernel checks whether it is already ready and queues an event, so EPOLLET plus EPOLLONESHOT re-armed after the read still gets notified; he notes this is undocumented.
facts.quote: At the time you call epoll_ctl to add or re-enable a fd, the kernel will always check whether the fd is already ready and queue an event for it if so. [1] To this extent, it acts 'level-triggered' regardless of whether you request level-triggered or edge-triggered mode. … And the behavior of checking for readiness at add/enable time doesn't seem to be documented, so it's hard to say if this is meant to be guaranteed.

facts.summary: Reader comment by HenrikH: an strace test on pipes on a 5.11 kernel, where data written while the descriptor was disarmed was reported by epoll_wait right after the EPOLL_CTL_MOD re-arm.
facts.quote: I just made a test of this using pipes on a 5.11 kernel … epoll_ctl(5, EPOLL_CTL_MOD, 3, {EPOLLIN|EPOLLONESHOT|EPOLLET, {u32=3, u64=2581266273925070851}}) = 0 … epoll_wait(5, [{EPOLLIN, {u32=3, u64=2581266273925070851}}], 1, -1) = 1

facts.summary: Reader comment by mkerrisk: EPOLLONESHOT dates from Linux 2.6.2 (2004); the flag added after the 2015 criticism is EPOLLEXCLUSIVE.
facts.quote: EPOLLONESHOT appeared in Linux 2.6.2, in 2004. I think you perhaps are thinking of EPOLLEXCLUSIVE.

facts.summary: Reader comment by HenrikH: EPOLLET re-arms on each new write (except pipes on the affected kernels), so with one epoll descriptor shared by threads a second thread gets EPOLLIN for the same descriptor while the first is still reading.
facts.quote: EPOLLET will re-arm when there is a new write (unless it was done on a pipe on v5-v15) so if you use the same epoll fd in multiple threads with EPOLLET then once thread A have called read and there is a new write, epoll will notify thread B about EPOLLIN on the same fd.

facts.summary: The post's author says early epoll did not support scaling across threads, and that EPOLLONESHOT and EPOLLEXCLUSIVE were the fixes.
facts.quote: Sometimes it is desirable to scale application by using multi threading. This was not supported by early implementations of epoll and was fixed by EPOLLONESHOT and EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flags.

facts.summary: Defensive rules the post gives: do not load-balance with epoll across threads, do not share the epoll descriptor or registered descriptors, and deregister before dup or close.
facts.quote: If you can you should avoid using epoll for load balancing across threads. Avoid sharing epoll file descriptor across threads. Avoid sharing epoll-registered file descriptors. Avoid forking, and if you must: close all epoll-registered file descriptors before calling execve. Explicitly deregister affected file descriptors from epoll set before calling dup/dup2/dup3 or close.

facts.summary: Before kernel 4.5, epoll could not be used to spread accept() over several workers.
facts.quote: Up until kernel 4.5 it wasn't possible to use epoll to scale out accepts.

facts.summary: Level-triggered epoll on a shared listening socket has the thundering-herd behaviour: every waiting worker wakes on each new connection.
facts.quote: This is because "level triggered" (aka: normal) epoll inherits the "thundering herd" semantics from select(). Without special flags, in level-triggered mode, all the workers will be woken up on each and every new connection.

facts.summary: Edge-triggered mode on a shared listening socket still causes needless wake-ups: a second thread wakes and gets EAGAIN because the first must keep calling accept() until EAGAIN.
facts.quote: Thread A: Must perform accept() since it does not know if kernel received one or more connections originally. It hopes to get EAGAIN, but gets another socket. … Thread B: Performs accept(), receives EAGAIN. This thread is confused. … The wake-up of Thread B was completely unnecessary and is confusing. Additionally, in edge triggered mode it's hard to avoid starvation

loc.heading: Edge triggered - unnecessary wake-up and starvation

facts.summary: Starvation: in the post's scenario a connection arriving while the socket is still readable emits no edge-triggered event, so one thread takes every connection and the load is not balanced.
facts.quote: Kernel: Receives third connection. The socket was "readable", still is "readable". Since we are in "edge triggered" mode, no event is emitted. … In this case the socket moved only once from "non-readable" to "readable" state. Since the socket is in edge-triggered mode, the kernel will wake up epoll exactly once. In this case all the connections will be received by Thread A and load balancing won't be achieved.

loc.heading: Edge triggered - unnecessary wake-up and starvation

facts.summary: For accept(), the post says the only scalable fix is kernel 4.5+ with level-triggered events and EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, which wakes a single thread per event.
facts.quote: The best and the only scalable approach is to use recent Kernel 4.5+ and use level-triggered events with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flag. This will ensure only one thread is woken for an event, avoid "thundering herd" issue and scale properly across multiple CPU's

facts.summary: Without EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, edge-triggered plus EPOLLONESHOT gives similar behaviour at the cost of one EPOLL_CTL_MOD re-arm per event, and only one worker accepts at a time.
facts.quote: Without EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, similar behavior it can be emulated with edge-triggered and EPOLLONESHOT, at a cost of one extra epoll_ctl() syscall after each event. This will distribute load across multiple CPU's properly, but at most one worker will call accept() at a time, limiting throughput. … Thread A: Performs epoll_ctl(EPOLL_CTL_MOD), this will reset the EPOLLONESHOT and re-arm the socket.

facts.summary: For read() on connected sockets shared by threads, EPOLLEXCLUSIVE does not help: a race can split one socket's data across two threads, which may reorder it without locking.
facts.quote: Additionally the EPOLLEXCLUSIVE won't help since there is a race condition possible. … In this situation the data is split across two threads and without using mutexes the data may be reordered.

facts.summary: Edge-triggered mode has the same race for read(): once the first thread drains the buffer the descriptor is re-armed, new data wakes a second thread, and the two threads read the same socket.
facts.quote: Kernel: the buffer is empty so the kernel arms the file descriptor again … Kernel: one thread is currently waiting in epoll_wait, wakes up Thread B … Thread B: performs read(2048) and gets 1 byte of data … Thread A: retries read(2048), which returns nothing, gets EAGAIN

facts.summary: The post's fix for the read() race is EPOLLONESHOT with a manual re-arm, which it says is the only way to deliver a descriptor's data to one thread.
facts.quote: The correct solution is to use EPOLLONESHOT and re-arm the file descriptor manually. This is the only way to guarantee that the data will be delivered to only one thread and avoid race conditions.

facts.summary: EPOLL_CTL_ADD registers a pair of the descriptor number and the underlying kernel object, and the registration lives as long as the kernel object, not the descriptor.
facts.quote: epoll_ctl(EPOLL_CTL_ADD) doesn't actually register a file descriptor. Instead it registers a tuple1 of a file descriptor and a pointer to underlying kernel object. Most confusingly the lifetime of an epoll subscription is not tied to the lifetime of a file descriptor. It's tied to the life of the kernel object.

facts.summary: close() removes the registration only when it drops the last reference to the kernel object; if another descriptor in any process still refers to it, events keep arriving for the closed descriptor.
facts.quote: Due to this implementation quirk calling close() on a file descriptor might or might not trigger epoll unsubscription. If the close call removes the last pointer to kernel object and causes the object to be freed, then it will cause epoll subscription cleanup. But if there are more pointers to kernel object, more file descriptors, in any process on the system, then close will not cause the epoll subscription cleanup. It is totally possible to receive events on previously closed file descriptors.

facts.summary: In the post's dup() example, after dup(rfd) and close(rfd), epoll_wait still reports an event for the closed rfd.
facts.quote: By calling dup, we kept the reference to the underlying "rfd" kernel object, we prevented it from being cleaned up. The thing is still subscribed to the epoll. epoll_wait will in fact terminate reporting an event on a dead handle "rfd".

facts.summary: Once the registered descriptor is closed, the registration cannot be removed: EPOLL_CTL_DEL needs a valid descriptor, and neither the closed one nor the dup works.
facts.quote: To make matters worse, you need a valid file descriptor handle to manage subscriptions on "epfd". After we called close(rfd), there is no way to unregister it from epfd! … Neither of these will work:

facts.summary: The post says the only recovery is to discard the epoll instance and rebuild every valid registration, and that EPOLL_CTL_DEL must always be called before close().
facts.quote: The only way froward is to trash the old "epfd", create new one and recreate all the valid subscriptions. … You always must always explicitly call epoll_ctl(EPOLL_CTL_DEL) before calling close().

facts.summary: Deregistering before close works only if you control all the code; an epoll wrapper library cannot stop its users from calling close themselves.
facts.quote: Explicitly deregistering file descriptors before close is nescesary and works well if you control all the code. In some cases though it may not be possible - for example when writing an epoll wrapper library. Sometimes it's impossible to forbid users from calling close themselves.

facts.summary: Eric Varsanyi (2003) reports that under edge-triggered epoll, data followed by a write-side shutdown() yields one EPOLLIN, so the server cannot tell that EOF also occurred; he proposes POLLRDHUP.
facts.quote: I'm proposing adding a new POLL event type (POLLRDHUP) as way to solve a new race introduced by having an edge triggered event mechanism (epoll). The problem occurs when a client writes data and then does a write side shutdown(). The server (using epoll) sees only one event for the read data ready and the read EOF condition and has no way to tell that an EOF occurred.

loc.heading: [Patch][RFC] epoll and half closed TCP connections

facts.summary: Varsanyi: level-triggered mode keeps reporting readiness while the socket is half-closed, but edge-triggered folds data and EOF into one event and loses an edge; an extra read() after a short read costs a syscall per event.
facts.quote: In a level triggered world this all just works because the read ready indication is driven back to the app as long as the socket state is half closed. The event driven epoll mechanism folds these two indications together and thus loses one 'edge'. … One would be tempted to issue an extra read() after getting back less than expected, but this is an extra system call on every read event

loc.heading: [Patch][RFC] epoll and half closed TCP connections

facts.summary: A reply signed Davide Libenzi states the short-read rule: when read/write returns fewer bytes than asked, stop processing the descriptor; later events arrive at the next epoll_wait(), with no blind spot.
facts.quote: When your read/write returns a lower number of bytes, it means that it is time to stop processing this fd. If events happened meanwhile, you will get them at the next epoll_wait(). If not, the next time they'll happen. There's no blind spot if you follow this simple rule, and you do not even have the extra syscall with EAGAIN.

loc.heading: Re: [Patch][RFC] epoll and half closed TCP connections

facts.summary: Varsanyi's timeline: data that arrives while the application is reading posts a second event, so after draining to EAGAIN the next epoll_wait() returns an EPOLLIN for an already-empty socket (the 'false positive' of the man page).
facts.quote: more read data added to socket … Socket posts a new read event to epfd … read() until short read with EAGAIN all data read from socket … epoll_wait() returns another EPOLLIN for socket and … clears it from epfd … This is your 'false positive' case in the epoll(4) man page.

loc.heading: Re: [Patch][RFC] epoll and half closed TCP connections

facts.summary: Libenzi's reply: in that false-positive case read() returns -1 with EAGAIN, not 0, so it cannot be mistaken for EOF.
facts.quote: read will return -1 with errno=EAGAIN in that case, not zero.

loc.heading: Re: [Patch][RFC] epoll and half closed TCP connections

facts.summary: Varsanyi then concedes the point and restates the remaining problem: without another read() you cannot tell whether an EOF came in on the same EPOLLIN event.
facts.quote: So the real issue (of the patch) is just the original thing I posted about: you can't tell w/o another read() syscall if an EOF has piggybacked in on an EPOLLIN event.

loc.heading: Re: [Patch][RFC] epoll and half closed TCP connections

facts.summary: Jamie Lokier: some descriptors return a short read while more data is still pending (ttys, some devices, TCP with urgent data and other cases), so read-until-EAGAIN is still required under edge-triggered mode.
facts.quote: That condition isn't strong enough for an edge-triggered event loop. Some kinds of fd return a short read when there is more data pending, due to boundaries - not a HUP condition, but read-until-EAGAIN is required nonetheless. Ttys do it, some devices do it, and TCP does it if there's urgent data (though POLLPRI should also be set) and under some other conditions.

loc.heading: POLLRDONCE optimisation for epoll users (was: epoll and half closed TCP connections)

facts.summary: Lokier: with edge-triggered epoll you must call read() until EAGAIN, because a single read() is not guaranteed to re-arm the event.
facts.quote: Otherwise, you must call read() repeatedly until you see EAGAIN, if you are using edge-triggered epoll. Simply calling read() once is not guaranteed to re-arm the event.

loc.heading: POLLRDONCE optimisation for epoll users (was: epoll and half closed TCP connections)

facts.summary: Lokier lists where the stop-at-short-read loop breaks (non-socket, non-TCP, kernel 2.5.75 or older, SO_RCVLOWAT below the read size, urgent data with OOBINLINE): it reads once where it needed to read until EAGAIN.
facts.quote: (a) fd isn't a socket … (b) fd isn't a TCP socket … (c) kernel version <= 2.5.75 … (d) SO_RCVLOWAT < s … (e) there is urgent data with OOBINLINE (I think) … The problem in cases (a)-(e) is your loop will call read() just once when it needs to call read() until it sees EAGAIN.

loc.heading: Re: POLLRDONCE optimisation for epoll users (was: epoll and half closed TCP connections)

conflicts.topic: Does edge-triggered mode fire only on an empty-to-non-empty transition?
conflicts.note: Torvalds's definition (quoted in the article) against reader comments by mkerrisk and HenrikH saying that epoll(7) and other file types wake on each new arrival

conflicts.topic: Does a listening socket in edge-triggered mode emit an event for a connection that arrives while it is still readable?
conflicts.note: the blog's accept-queue scenario says no event; the reader comments say stream sockets and new writes re-arm EPOLLET. Listening and connected sockets may differ, and neither side shows a test of a listening socket

conflicts.topic: Is there a lost-event race when re-arming an EPOLLONESHOT descriptor with EPOLL_CTL_MOD?
conflicts.note: NYKevin says re-arming leaves a race; comex and HenrikH say re-arm checks readiness and HenrikH shows a 5.11 strace; comex adds that this is undocumented

conflicts.topic: Does a short read mean the descriptor is drained under edge-triggered mode?
conflicts.note: Libenzi's stop-at-short-read rule against Lokier's list of descriptors and conditions where a short read leaves data pending

conflicts.topic: Do EPOLLONESHOT and EPOLLEXCLUSIVE fix multi-threaded epoll?
conflicts.note: same post: the general claim drops the condition that EPOLLEXCLUSIVE does not fix the read() race on connected sockets, only accept()
